title: Dig up the root (338–343)
hookLine: a tree cut down grows again if the root is sound; so suffering returns while craving lives

cards: Anyone who has cut down a stubborn bush knows what happens next spring. The stump looks finished, and then little green shoots come up all around it. You cut them, and they come back.

The trunk was never the problem. The roots were still alive under the ground, patient and well fed. It's the same with a habit you thought you'd beaten, a temper you thought you'd outgrown, a worry you thought was gone.

teach.b: Verse three hundred thirty-eight puts it plainly. A tree that's been cut down will grow again, as long as its root is unharmed.
In the same way, as long as the craving underneath hasn't been uprooted, suffering keeps coming back, again and again. The verse right before it gives a farmer's picture.
In India, people dig up a tough grass called birana to get at its root, which is fragrant and valuable. That root is known today as vetiver, used in perfumes and cooling mats.
So digging up the root isn't only destruction: you dig because what's underneath matters.

teach.h: THIRTY-SIX STREAMS, THE HARE IN THE SNARE.
teach.b: Then the verses map the roots: thirty-six streams of craving, all running toward pleasure, and channels running everywhere, with the creeper sprouting up wherever they reach.

When you see the creeper springing up, the text says, cut its root with wisdom. Then a picture you can almost see: people driven by thirst run about like a snared hare, held in fetters, suffering again and again.

The root isn't the thing you crave: not the phone, the snack or the praise. The root is the craving itself, and the not-seeing that feeds it. That's why the text says to cut it with wisdom, not with force.
Chopping the trunk is willpower, and it's useful. Digging the root is understanding why, and that's what stops the shoots in spring.

how: In Buddhist teaching, craving is uprooted by insight rather than willpower alone; meditators investigate what lies beneath a recurring desire, and teachers often use the verse of the tree that grows back.

o: the trunk, chopped down by willpower
a seed planted for a better rebirth
the root, where craving is cut with wisdom

games.q: match each piece of today's verses.
p: grows again while the root lives
dug up for its fragrant root

s: the verses say the root is the thing you crave
the root is the craving itself, and the not-seeing that feeds it.
birana grass has a fragrant root people dig up
the root is known today as vetiver.
the text says to cut the creeper's root with wisdom
when you see it springing up, cut its root with wisdom.

games.q: you've deleted the same app three times, and each time it finds its way back onto your phone. what do today's verses suggest?
o: look for the root: what you're really wanting underneath.
accept that it's just who you are.
games.why: a tree cut down grows again while its root is sound; the verses say to cut the root with wisdom, which means understanding the craving.

practice: Bring to mind one craving that keeps sprouting back, and dig gently, one layer at a time: what do I want when I want this, and under that, what do I want? Maybe comfort, or rest, or to feel less alone.
Don't force an answer; keep asking softly, then let the question rest and come back to the breath.

wordCard.voice: Mūla. Root: a cut tree grows again while its root lives, so cut craving at the root, with wisdom, not force.

orig.note: Pali mūla: root; verse 338 speaks of a tree whose root is unharmed.

carryVoice: Your line: dig the root. Under every shoot that comes back, there's a living root. See you tomorrow.
